title: The development of Tunnel
titleCn: 英法海底隧道的发展史

paragraphs.text: You will hear a lecture about the development of the tunnel linking France and England.
First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

The strip of sea separating France and England, which in English is simply called the Channel, is only thirty-four kilometers across at the shortest point. But in the days of sailing ships, the strong currents and fierce storms made it difficult to cross.
In favorable conditions, the voyage took six or seven hours, but it could equally well take days or even a week.

In seventeen fifty, a competition was launched in the city of Amiens in northern France for a scheme that would improve trade links between the two nations. The committee awarded the prize to an engineer who proposed a tunnel, though the technology and manpower that it required were simply not available at the time.

Half a century later, the idea resurfaced. In eighteen oh two, during a break in hostilities in the war between France and England, a French mining engineer put forward another scheme for a tunnel. The scheme was supported by the peace party among English politicians, but the resumption of war dashed their hopes.

By eighteen fifty, Europe was much more industrialized. In eighteen sixty-seven, a French hydrographic engineer presented his government with a proposal for a tunnel to carry trains. As regards the engineering, this was quite feasible. Tunnels through the Alps were under construction, and the Suez Canal was nearing completion.
A committee was set up in the following year to explore the possibility, and in eighteen eighty, they started excavating to build tunnels from both coasts.
But British public opinion turned against the idea, and in eighteen eighty-two, the government put a stop to the digging.

The notion of a fixed link didn't go away, however. And in the nineteen twenties, the idea was put forward in Britain of a tunnel with its entrance half a kilometer out to sea, linked to the coast by a bridge. But in the economic climate of the nineteen thirties, neither country could afford the vast undertaking of any sort of tunnel.

During the nineteen fifties, the idea was again considered seriously. But it was not until nineteen eighty-five that it was finally agreed, and the two governments staged a competition for the best proposal.
The committee came down in favor of the tunnel for trains and shuttles only. The reasons that were given largely centered on the finances, which were considered to be the soundest put forward.

It was also thought that compared with the alternative options, the technical risks of the tunnel were considerably reduced, not least because as a pure engineering exercise, it called for little in the way of innovative technology. In fact, solving logistical, environmental, and other problems created more headaches than the engineering.
The tunnel was regarded as the safest way for people to get across the Channel, and unlike a bridge, it wouldn't impede shipping.

Excavation of three tunnels started in nineteen eighty-seven from both sides at once, and the first one to form a continuous link between the two countries reached its breakthrough point in December nineteen ninety, just to the French side of the international border. The tunnel was eventually opened to traffic in nineteen ninety-four.

The system consists of three tunnels. The two outer tunnels, which carry the shuttles and trains, are known as running tunnels. They're each separated by eight meters of rock from the smaller service tunnel, which goes along the middle between them and is used for maintenance.
Every three hundred and seventy-five meters, the three tunnels are linked by cross passages, which provide ventilation and easy access for maintenance.
Once the high-speed train link between the English coast and London is-
That is the end of part four. You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
